# **Molecular Movement in the Cells and Across Cell Membranes**

## **Pre-Lab Activity 5.1: Questions**

**Lab Objectives: Cell Membranes, Diffusion, and Osmosis**

By the end of this lab, students will be able to:

1.  Describe the structure and function of the cell membrane.

2.  Explain the concepts of diffusion and osmosis.

3.  Distinguish between passive transport and active transport.

4.  Define hypertonic, hypotonic, and isotonic solutions.

5.  Predict the movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane.

6.  Perform an osmosis experiment using dialysis tubing.

7.  Measure and record changes in mass over time.

8.  Analyze data to determine the direction of water movement.

9.  Compare how plant and animal cells respond to different solutions.

10. Explain the role of the cell wall in plant cell responses to osmosis.

## **Introduction: Molecular Movement in the Cells and Across Cell Membranes**

> All cells are enclosed by membranes which provide a semi-permeable barrier between the internal contents of the cell and its external environment. Cells must be able to regulate the movement of molecules or ions (i.e., amino acids, sugars, O~2~) so that their concentrations do not disrupt cell metabolic processes. In addition to regulating what contents may enter or exit the cell, the cell membrane plays a role in a few other functions, including communication, binding, and adhering to adjacent cells. Properties of the cell membrane can be determined by exposing red blood cells to different solutions (i.e., different "environments") and observing the appearance of cells under a microscope. The cell may, for example, lyse due to the influx of water. More specifically, we will be looking at how animal cells (red blood cells) and plant cells respond differently to distinct types of solutions.
>
> ***Diffusion***
>
> ![](data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAMYAAAACAQMAAAA5LDG8AAAABlBMVEUAAAD///+l2Z/dAAAAAWJLR0QAiAUdSAAAAAlwSFlzAAAOxAAADsQBlSsOGwAAAA1JREFUCJljYCAZMAMAADcABBjomQAAAAAASUVORK5CYII=){width="0.6599989063867017in" height="6.666666666666667e-3in"}
>
> Molecules can pass a cell membrane using different means of transport. One such means is **passive transport**; in which case the laws of thermodynamics dictate the flow of molecules. In passive transport, no added energy (ATP) is necessary for the movement of molecules as they move along their **concentration gradient**, passing from high to low concentration. There are several types of passive transport, including diffusion and osmosis.
>
> Some, but not all, of the traffic across the membranes of cells occurs by diffusion. **Diffusion** is the movement of molecules from an area of greater to an area of lesser concentration. Molecules are in motion constantly due to their natural movement caused by thermal agitation (**Brownian Motion**), and they bounce off each other and disperse themselves in an area until equilibrium is reached. **Equilibrium** means that the molecules have an equal distribution across the medium. Keep in mind that each particle is exhibiting random motion--- you cannot predict which way an individual particle will move---but you can predict the net movement of the collection of particles.
>
> As biological membranes are selectively permeable, some substances can freely diffuse through the membrane more easily than others. This is due to the contrasting properties of the phospholipid bilayer that makes up the cell membrane, as it includes both polar and nonpolar regions. Moreover, substances that move through the membrane can do so at different rates. Hydrophobic or non-polar molecules, such as hydrocarbons, oxygen, and carbon dioxide, can dissolve in the membrane and cross it with ease due to the hydrophobic nature of the membrane. Conversely, most hydrophilic molecules, such as ions and polar molecules, cannot pass through the membrane.
>
> **Osmosis**
>
> **Osmosis** is a special case of passive transport that deals with the diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane. Osmosis depends upon the concentration of solutes in a solution. A solution is made up of a solvent, the substance that does the dissolving, and a solute, the substance that is being dissolved. In the case of osmosis, the solvent is water. A Solute is a substance, such as sugar or salt that is dissolved in the water.
>
> In comparing two solutions of unequal solute concentration, the solution with a greater concentration of solutes is said to be **hypertonic.** The solution with the lesser solute concentration is **hypotonic**. These are relative terms that are only meaningful in a comparative sense. For example, tap water is hypertonic to distilled water, but hypotonic to seawater. In other words, tap water has a higher concentration of solutes than distilled water, but a lower concentration than seawater. Solutions of equal solute concentration are said to be **isotonic.**
>
> If a cell is placed in an environment which is isotonic, an environment of equal solute concentration, then there is no concentration gradient. Without such a gradient, there will be no net flow of water across the membrane.
>
> If a cell is placed in a hypotonic environment, then there is a lower solute concentration surrounding the cell than within the cell. Whenever the solute concentration is lower, the concentration of free water molecules is higher. Therefore, water will diffuse alongdown its concentration gradient from an area of higher concentration (outside the cell) to an area of lower concentration (inside the cell). The added pressure that develops because osmosis is occurring is called **hydrostatic (**or **turgor) pressure.** This pressure may increase the point of opposing the entry of more water by osmosis (in which case it is equal to **osmotic pressure),** or this pressure may cause the membrane to rupture before such a point is reached.
>
> Conversely, a cell placed in a hypertonic environment is surrounded by solution which is higher in solutes, hence lower in free water molecules. In this case, the free water concentration is greater inside the cell than outside, so the water flows out of the cell.
>
> Plant and animal cells will respond differently in hypertonic, hypotonic, and isotonic solutions. This is primarily due to the presence of a cell wall in plant cells, which is absent from animal cells. For example, an animal cell (such as a red blood cell) will **lyse** (burst open) in a hypotonic solution due to the movement of water molecules into the cell. A plant cell placed into a hypotonic solution is considered turgid, however, and will not lyse due to the presence of the cell wall.

**\

## **Procedure**

A.  Simple Diffusion in Agar

> Agar is a semi-solid substance made of long chains of molecules arranged in a random pattern. Because of this structure, it has many small pores and fewer large ones. Smaller molecules can diffuse through agar more easily because they can pass through these pores, while larger molecules move more slowly and may become trapped. In this experiment, you will compare how different substances diffuse through agar.

1.  Materials: Obtain the following:

    a.  2 agar plates

    b.  Ruler

        i.  Only a small portion is used to cut your holes in the agar so you may have to cut a whole straw in half

    c.  Drinking straw

    d.  Stains: three of the following

    <!-- -->

    1.  Methylene Blue

    2.  Neutral Red

    3.  Crystal Violet

    4.  Methyl Green

        2.  When a cell is exposed to an environment that has a greater concentration of solute than is in the cell, the cell loses water by osmosis. Place a drop of 10% NaCl solution just touching one side of the cover glass. Use a small piece of paper towel or lens paper to draw the original water out from the opposite side of the cover glass. This procedure will draw the salt solution under the cover glass and surround the leaf with salt water. Repeat the addition of a drop of NaCl and the removal of water from under the cover glass. Again, examine the cells of the *Elodea* leaf.

![](data:image/png;base64,){width="3.458018372703412in" height="1.6857841207349082in"}

A figure showing how to expose Elodea leaf cells to a hypertonic solution: a drop of sodium chloride (NaCl) solution is placed at one edge of a microscope cover glass, while a paper towel draws out water from the opposite edge, pulling the salt solution underneath the cover glass and around the leaf. This process is repeated to fully bathe the cells in salt solution, causing them to lose water by osmosis before being viewed again under the microscope.

## **Appendix: Key Terms and Definitions for the Osmosis and the Cell Lab**

  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Term**                        **Definition**
  ------------------------------- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Active Transport                The movement of substances across a cell membrane against their concentration gradient, requiring energy (ATP).

  ATP (Adenosine Triphosphate)    The primary energy-carrying molecule used by cells to power processes such as active transport.

  Brownian Motion                 The random movement of particles in a fluid is caused by collisions with other fast-moving molecules.

  Cell Membrane                   A selectively permeable barrier composed of a phospholipid bilayer that regulates what enters and exits the cell.

  Cell Wall                       A rigid outer layer found in plant cells that provides structure and prevents over-expansion during water uptake.

  Centrioles                      Cylindrical structures involved in organizing microtubules and assisting in cell division in animal cells. 

  Chromatin                       A complex of DNA and proteins (histones) that form chromosomes and help regulate gene expression. 

  Chromosomes                     Threadlike structures made of DNA that carry genetic information, especially visible during cell division. 

  Cilia                           Short, hair-like structures that move fluid or substances across the cell surface. 

  Concentration Gradient          The difference in the concentration of a substance between two areas.

  Cytoplasm (cytosol)             The gel-like substance inside the cell where organelles are suspended and many metabolic reactions occur. 

  Cytoskeleton                    A network of protein filaments that provides structural support, shape, and movement for the cell. 

  Dialysis Tubing                 A semi-permeable membrane used in experiments to model how substances move across cell membranes.

  Diffusion                       The passive movement of molecules from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration.

  Equilibrium                     A state in which molecules are evenly distributed, resulting in no net movement.

  Flagellum                       A long, whip-like structure that enables cell movement (e.g., sperm cell motility). 

  Golgi apparatus                 An organelle that modifies, sorts, and packages proteins and lipids for transport. 

  Hypertonic Solution             A solution with a higher solute concentration than the cell, causing water to move out of the cell.

  Hypotonic Solution              A solution with a lower solute concentration than the cell, causing water to move into the cell.

  Isotonic Solution               A solution with equal solute concentration inside and outside the cell, resulting in no net water movement.

  Lysosome                        A membrane-bound organelle containing digestive enzymes that break down waste materials and cellular debris. 

  Mass Change                     A measurable increase or decrease in mass used to determine water movement during osmosis experiments.

  Microvilli                      Small, finger-like projections that increase surface area for absorption, commonly found in intestinal cells. 

  Mitochondria                    Organelles that generate energy (ATP) through cellular respiration; often called the cell's \'powerhouse.\' 

  Nucleus                         A membrane-bound organelle that contains the cell's DNA and controls cellular activities. 

  Nuclear envelope                A double membrane that surrounds the nucleus, containing pores that regulate material exchange. 

  Nucleolus                       A dense region within the nucleus where ribosomal RNA (rRNA) is produced, and ribosome assembly begins. 

  Osmosis                         The passive movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane from an area of lower solute concentration to higher solute concentration.

  Passive Transport               The movement of substances across a membrane without the use of cellular energy, following the concentration gradient.

  Peroxisome                      An organelle containing enzymes that break down fatty acids and detoxify harmful substances using oxygen. 

  Phospholipid Bilayer            The double layer of phospholipids that forms the basic structure of the cell membrane, with hydrophilic heads and hydrophobic tails.

  Red Blood Cells                 Animal cells are often used in experiments to observe membrane behavior in different solutions.

  Ribosome                        A small organelle responsible for protein synthesis, found free in the cytosol or attached to rough ER. 

  Rough endoplasmic reticulum     A membrane network studded with ribosomes involved in protein synthesis and folding. 

  Selective Permeability          The property of a membrane that allows some substances to pass while restricting others.

  Smooth endoplasmic reticulum    A membrane network without ribosomes involved in lipid synthesis and detoxification. 

  Solute                          A substance that is dissolved in a solution.

  Solvent                         The substance (often water) that dissolves the solute to form a solution.

  Transport Mechanism             Any process that allows substances to move across the cell membrane (e.g., diffusion, osmosis, active transport).

  Turgor Pressure                 The pressure exerted by water inside a plant cell against the cell wall, helping maintain structure.
  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
